analysis.one_liner: Lets small employers pool together and individuals use tax credits to buy private health insurance, with some options freed from state rules.
analysis.headline: Introduced in March 1999 with 5 Republican cosponsors, the bill was sent to three House committees and never received a committee or floor vote before the 106th Congress ended in January 2001.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would create 'HealthMarts' and association health plans: purchasing pools that let small employers band together to buy private health insurance for their workers, with certain coverage options exempt from state benefit requirements. It would also give individuals a refundable tax credit for buying health coverage and lift limits on medical savings accounts. It was referred to three committees in March 1999 and died there without ever getting a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Small employers and their employees, who could pool through trade associations or HealthMarts to buy coverage at group rates instead of small-group prices. Uninsured individuals, who could claim a refundable tax credit toward buying coverage. Self-employed people and others who could use expanded medical savings accounts.

how_it_helps.text: Small employers could join association health plans sponsored by trade associations, industry groups, or chambers of commerce, and contribution rates for participating small employers could not vary based on the employer's own claims experience or type of business [S3].
HealthMarts would provide full portability: a worker who changes employers but stays in the same HealthMart keeps creditable coverage rather than starting over [S2].
The bill creates a refundable tax credit for individuals who purchase qualified health coverage [S2].

It lifts the statutory cap on how many taxpayers can open medical savings accounts, increases the allowable deduction, lowers the deductible threshold, and lets MSAs be offered through employer cafeteria plans [S2].

Coverage offered through a HealthMart or association plan could not deny enrollment based on health status, and each must offer at least four coverage options, at least one of them a non-network plan [S2].
HealthMarts must publish consumer information on the scope, cost, and enrollee satisfaction of every coverage option they offer [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers would fund the refundable coverage credits and a new Association Health Plan Fund that backstops financially troubled plans. State governments would lose regulatory authority: state benefit-mandate laws and 'fictitious group' rules would be superseded for HealthMart coverage, and two of every four coverage options would be exempt from state benefit mandates.

drawbacks.text: State benefit-requirement laws are superseded for coverage sold through HealthMarts, and at least two of the four required coverage options would be exempt from all state benefit mandates — mandates that typically require things like maternity care, mental health coverage, or specific provider access [S3].
Association plans could offer two options meeting a federal 'model benefits package' in place of state-mandated benefits, substituting a federal floor for stricter state rules [S3].
An employer contracting with a HealthMart agrees not to sponsor any other health coverage for its employees, so workers would be locked into the HealthMart channel [S3].

The bill's own solvency machinery — required reserves, excess/stop-loss insurance, a $5,000-per-plan annual payment into a federal fund, mandatory termination procedures, and federal trusteeship of insolvent plans — anticipates that association plans could fail financially and need federal backstopping [S3].
The bill narrows the existing self-employed health insurance deduction so it would apply only to long-term care insurance, replacing it with the new purchase credit [S2].

When healthier employer groups migrate into lightly regulated association plans, the costlier risk pools left behind in state-regulated markets can see premiums rise — a standard criticism of association health plan proposals, which the bill's rate-adjustment and solvency provisions implicitly acknowledge [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For small employers and some uninsured individuals, pooling and a refundable credit could genuinely lower the cost of coverage, and portability provisions would help workers who switch jobs. But the way the savings are achieved matters: the bill gets there partly by preempting state benefit mandates and letting some options skip state rules entirely, which shifts regulatory protection from states to federal minimums and to plan-by-plan design choices. The extensive solvency and federal-fund provisions are an honest signal that Congress expected some association plans to fail. The bill was never debated or amended in public, so its real-world balance was never tested.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to three House committees when introduced in March 1999, passed along to two subcommittees in April, and none of them ever reported it out — it died when the 106th Congress ended in January 2001.

narrative.text: Rep. Charlie Norwood and original cosponsors including Majority Leader Dick Armey introduced the bill on March 16, 1999 [S3].
It was referred to the Committee on Commerce and additionally to the Committees on Education and the Workforce and Ways and Means [S5].
In April 1999 it was referred to the Commerce Subcommittee on Health and Environment and the Education Subcommittee on Employer-Employee Relations [S5].
No committee reported the bill, no markup or floor vote is recorded, and no further action appears before the Congress ended on January 3, 2001 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Nothing changed, so state insurance regulators and the existing small-group insurance market kept operating under current rules. Small employers, the uninsured, and insurers lost the new channels the bill would have created.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The status quo and state regulators

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all five cosponsors were Republicans, and Republicans controlled all three committees of referral, but no vote was ever taken, so no one ever had to go on record for or against it.

industries.note: All coverage would flow through state-licensed insurers and HMOs, with HealthMart boards required to include representatives of underwriting entities — locking private insurers in as the permanent channel for the new purchasing pools. Insurers would gain new group markets, though two of every four coverage options would be exempt from state benefit mandates, reducing the rules that apply to their products [S3].

Small employers could pool through trade associations, professional groups, or chambers of commerce to buy coverage at rates that could not vary by their own claims experience, and associations would gain a certified federal role as plan sponsors [S3].

State benefit-mandate laws, grouping requirements, and other rules that preclude HealthMart or association plan offerings would be superseded, shifting regulatory authority from states to federal administrators [S3].
The bill requires state-licensed agents to distribute non-health benefit options to small employers in a manner comparable to health coverage distribution, protecting their commission channel [S3].
